title: Cannabis and Fitness: Timing, Formats and Safety
h1: Working Out and Cannabis: Timing, Formats and Safety for Active Adults
metaDescription: Cannabis and fitness for adults 21+: what research shows, onset and duration by format, label checks, heart rate and coordination cautions, and common mistakes.
excerpt: A timing-first look at cannabis and exercise for adults 21+: what studies have found, how long each format takes to start and fade, and the safety basics to keep in mind.
keyTakeaways: Research hasn't shown that THC improves aerobic performance or strength, and a 2025 trial found CBD didn't change endurance or muscle-damage markers.
Cannabis can speed up your heart, push up your blood pressure and dull your coordination, so skip it before hard, technical or risky exercise.
Inhaled cannabis starts within minutes and fades in a few hours; with edibles, expect a wait of up to 2 hours and effects that can run for 12.
Michigan labels show THC and CBD amounts plus an activation time, two details that help you plan around a workout.
Michigan bans cannabis use in public places, so keep it at home, and never drive after using.
body:
Cannabis and fitness can share your week, but rarely the same hour. Research hasn't shown that cannabis makes you faster or stronger, and THC can push your heart rate and blood pressure up and blunt your coordination. That makes timing and format the decisions that matter most. Here's what studies have found, how to plan around workouts and rest days, how long each format takes to start and fade, and the safety basics. We wrote it for adults 21 and over, and it isn't medical advice: if you have a heart condition, take medications or are pregnant, talk with a clinician first.

## Cannabis and fitness: what research does and doesn't show

Plenty of active adults are curious about combining cannabis and exercise, but the research is thin, and it doesn't point toward better performance.

- **No boost in performance.** A 2017 systematic review found only 15 published studies that tested THC alongside an exercise protocol. None showed an improvement in aerobic performance, and strength was probably reduced. In two studies, cannabis brought on angina, a type of chest pain, at a lower workload, and some people couldn't finish an exercise test because of side effects.
- **CBD and recovery.** Many athletes say they use CBD to help them recover, but controlled trials haven't backed that up. In a 2025 University of Sydney trial, 25 trained runners took 50 mg or 300 mg of CBD, or a placebo, before an hour-long treadmill run followed by a run to exhaustion. CBD didn't change how hard the run felt, how long they lasted or blood markers of muscle damage.
- **Big gaps remain.** Most studies are small, short and done in labs, so they can't predict how cannabis will affect your own workout.

The practical takeaway: plan around cannabis's effects instead of expecting it to help your training.

## Planning around your week: before, after, rest days and weekends

### Before exercise

Skip cannabis before anything hard, technical or risky: heavy lifting, sprints, climbing, contact sports, cycling in traffic or swimming. Cannabis can make your heart beat faster and raise your blood pressure right after use, and it impairs the thinking and coordination skills you'd need to drive. You lean on those same skills on a bike, on a climbing wall or under a barbell.

### After exercise

If you choose to use cannabis after a workout, wait until you've cooled down, had some water and eaten. Let your heart rate settle first, since cannabis can push it back up. Keep the amount small, and don't drive home from the gym after using. Inhaled effects usually take about three to four hours to fade, so leave that window free of anything that needs a clear head.

### Rest days

Rest days are the simplest fit. Nothing is on the training calendar, so a free evening at home is easy to set aside.

### Weekend outings

For hikes, paddles and long walks, save cannabis for when you're back home. Michigan law doesn't permit cannabis use in public places, and an edible taken before you head out can still be building hours later, far from the car. The same goes on the water and in the snow: state law bars using cannabis while operating a motorboat, snowmobile or off-road vehicle.

### A sample week

| Day | Training | Where cannabis fits |
|---|---|---|
| Hard training day | Strength work, intervals or a long run | Not before; if at all, a small amount in the evening once you've cooled down and eaten |
| Easy day | A walk, an easy ride or gentle yoga | Not before; evening only |
| Rest day | None | Your simplest window, at a time with nowhere to be |
| Weekend outing | A hike, a paddle or a long walk | After you're home, never on the trail or the water |
| Morning after an evening edible | An early session on the calendar | Keep it easy or move it, since drowsiness can linger |

## Formats and timing, from flower and vapes to edibles and topicals

Each format changes how fast effects arrive and how long they stay.

- **Flower and pre-rolls.** Smoked cannabis is usually felt within minutes. Smoke is also hard on your lungs: the CDC notes that cannabis smoke contains many of the same substances found in tobacco smoke.
- **Vapes.** Also felt within minutes. Vape oils are concentrated, so a single puff can be stronger than you expect.
- **Edibles.** Effects usually begin 30 minutes to 2 hours after eating, can take up to 4 hours to peak and can last up to 12 hours.
- **Drinks.** Cannabis drinks are swallowed, so plan on edible timing unless the label's activation time says otherwise.
- **Tinctures.** Held under the tongue, they're thought to act faster than edibles, though the evidence is mixed. Whatever you swallow acts more like an edible.
- **Topicals.** Lotions, balms and creams don't seem to cause a high, and research on what they can do is limited. Some people react to them with itching, swelling or hives, so try a small patch of skin first. Transdermal patches are a different product, designed to carry cannabinoids through the skin. Our guide to [cannabis topicals](/blog/guide-to-cannabis-topicals/) explains the difference.

## Onset and duration windows explained

| Format | Effects usually start | How long they can last |
|---|---|---|
| Smoked or vaped | Within about 10 minutes, peaking in the first hour | About 3 to 4 hours |
| Edibles and drinks | Usually 30 to 120 minutes; the peak can take up to 4 hours | Up to 12 hours; drowsiness can hang on for up to a day |
| Tinctures | Varies; the evidence is mixed | Depends on how much is swallowed |
| Topicals | Don't seem to cause a high | Not applicable |

Why the big gap? Inhaled THC reaches your bloodstream within minutes. Swallowed THC is absorbed more slowly and less predictably, because it's broken down in the stomach and gut and processed by the liver first. Blood levels usually peak one to three hours after eating, and for some people as late as four to six hours.

What that means for your training:

- An edible taken at lunch can still be working during an evening workout.
- An evening edible can leave you groggy the next morning, so don't schedule a hard early session after one.
- Inhaled effects fade sooner, but you're still impaired while you feel them.
- Taking more because an edible hasn't kicked in yet is a common way to end up with far more than you planned.

Our comparison of [fast-acting cannabis products](/blog/best-fast-acting-cannabis-products/) goes deeper on onset by format.

## Matching formats to routines

Everyone's week looks different. These examples are about timing, not promised effects.

- **Winding down after an evening workout.** Cool down, eat and rehydrate first. A small inhaled amount fades within a few hours, while a low-dose edible commits you to a long, quiet evening at home.
- **Long weekend walks.** Leave cannabis for after you're home. Public use isn't allowed, and an edible's long tail is hard to manage on the trail.
- **Stretching sessions at home.** If you do gentle stretching or mobility work on a rest day, keep amounts small and skip poses that test your balance.
- **Group classes and team play.** Show up clear-headed. Instructors, teammates and spotters count on you to move safely.
- **Experienced consumers.** Tolerance can change how strongly you feel cannabis, but it doesn't make heavy or technical training safe while you're impaired. Keep cannabis and hard sessions on separate days.

## Label checks: THC and CBD per serving, format and onset notes

Michigan labels give you most of what you need to plan your timing:

- **THC and CBD content.** With edibles and drinks, look at both the milligrams in one serving and the package total. A bar or bottle can hold several servings.
- **Activation time.** Michigan labels include an activation time, a note on how long effects may take to begin.
- **Format.** Swallowed products start slowly and last longer; inhaled products start fast and fade sooner.
- **Testing details.** The label tells you where and when the batch was tested.
- **CBD-forward products.** CBD doesn't cause a high, but CBD products may still hold some THC, so check that number as well.

Do the math before you plan your day. A chocolate bar labeled 100 mg of THC and scored into 10 pieces holds about 10 mg per piece, and that number tells you more than the size of the bite. The same goes for pre-rolls: the label lists the net weight, and you don't have to finish one in a sitting.

Curious what CBD research has and hasn't shown? Our [CBD evidence guide](/blog/cbd-benefits/) covers it.

## Safety: heart rate, balance, hydration and heat

- **Heart rate and blood pressure.** Cannabis can make your heart beat faster and raise your blood pressure immediately after use, according to the CDC. Exercise does the same, so stacking the two adds strain. If you have a heart condition or high blood pressure, talk with your doctor before using cannabis at all.
- **Balance and coordination.** Cannabis impairs the thinking and motor skills needed to drive, and you rely on those same skills for balance, timing and quick reactions during exercise.
- **Hydration.** Drink water before, during and after exercise, as you would anyway. Our article on [whether cannabis dehydrates you](/blog/does-weed-dehydrate-you/) looks at what the research says.
- **Heat.** Hot, humid days already add strain to your heart during exercise. If you've used cannabis, skip hard outdoor sessions in the heat.
- **Cold and dark.** Icy sidewalks and early winter sunsets already ask a lot of your balance and attention, so save Michigan winter runs and rides for clear-headed days.
- **Medications and pregnancy.** CBD can change how some medicines work, and Michigan cannabis labels carry a pregnancy and breastfeeding warning. Talk with a clinician first.
- **Warning signs.** If you feel faint, dizzy or short of breath, or have chest pain, stop and get medical help.

## Mistakes active consumers make

- **Using before heavy, technical or risky training.** Save cannabis for after the session or for rest days.
- **Timing an edible badly.** An edible taken before a workout may peak mid-session, or in the car on the way home.
- **Re-dosing too soon.** Wait a full 2 hours after an edible before you decide on more.
- **Mixing with alcohol.** Alcohol adds to cannabis's impairment.
- **Driving after using.** Michigan law makes it illegal to drive while under the influence of marijuana.
- **Using in public.** Public use isn't permitted in Michigan, so keep cannabis at home.
- **Counting on CBD for recovery.** A 2025 controlled trial in trained runners found no change in exertion, endurance or markers of muscle damage.
- **Skipping the basics.** Sleep, food and water are the foundation of training, and no product replaces them.

If you compete, check your sport's anti-doping rules; our article on [cannabis in sports](/blog/cannabis-in-sports/) covers how leagues and testing bodies handle it.

Curious about a label or format? Ask our budtenders at your nearest [Michigan store](/dispensary-locations/). For anything about your health, your clinician is the one to ask. 21+ only, or 18+ with a medical marijuana card. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: Is it safe to use cannabis before working out?
faq.a: It's not a good idea before hard, technical or risky exercise. Cannabis can quicken your pulse and lift your blood pressure soon after use, it dulls coordination, and a review of exercise studies found no performance benefit from THC. If you have a heart condition or take any medicines, check with your doctor first.

There's no good evidence that it does. In a 2025 trial, trained runners who took 50 mg or 300 mg of CBD before a long run showed no change in exertion, endurance or blood markers of muscle damage compared with a placebo. CBD can also interact with some medications, so check with a clinician before trying it.

faq.q: Do cannabis topicals get you high?
faq.a: Lotions, balms and creams don't seem to cause a high, according to a Canadian review of the research. Transdermal patches are another story: they use the skin as a route into the bloodstream, so read the label closely. Research on what topicals can do is limited, so be skeptical of bold claims on a package.

faq.q: How long after an edible can I exercise?
faq.a: Wait until the effects have fully worn off. Edibles usually start working within 30 minutes to 2 hours, can take up to 4 hours to peak and can last up to 12 hours; drowsiness may linger into the next day. In practice, that often means saving hard or technical training for another day. If you wake up groggy after an evening edible, swap a hard session for an easy walk.
